title: Zhang Ya-Qin: Information Intelligence Tops Out in Five Years, Humanoid Robots Need Another Ten
dek: He splits AGI into three layers — information, physical, biological: information intelligence reaches human level within five years, but that is the IQ of a brain; reading ten thousand books still won't teach you to swim, and physical intelligence has only just begun.
why: A timetable and classification framework from an academician; medium information density, and the second half — on lifespan and the extension of the species — is more interesting than the first.
who: Founders and investors watching the AGI roadmap and the pace at which autonomous driving and embodied intelligence land; anyone who wants a timetable and classification framework from an academician.
skip: The book recommendations after 51:27 can be skipped; they are unrelated to the main argument.

points.h: A first-rate research institute cannot be measured by quantitative assessment
points.body: Zhang Ya-Qin recalls that when Microsoft Research China was setting its goals, the consultant and Nobel laureate Rodger Ely gave a counterintuitive answer: how do we measure whether we are first-rate? "When you are not worrying about this question, when you are not talking about this question, you have become first-rate." He later ran into the same sentence again on ChatGPT — when does the Turing test count as passed? "When you pass it, you'll know." From this he derived three goals for the institute: recruit first-rate talent, set long-term directions, and cultivate first-rate research talent — and for the first two or three years, 80% of the time went into finding people.

points.h: Running a research institute today, the hard part isn't hiring but choosing topics
points.body: Zhang Ya-Qin says that compared with 1998, doing AIR now is actually "relatively easy" — China already has world-class research results and talent, and within the Tsinghua environment recruiting good teachers and good students is not a problem. The real difficulty has shifted: in the past Microsoft Research did whatever the people it found wanted to do, "they did whatever they liked," and without a leading figure in a field you couldn't build it; now you can find people in any direction, so you have to choose the direction yourself. AIR therefore chose three vertical directions: intelligent transportation, IoT, and AI plus life sciences — in today's language, robotics, embodied intelligence, biological intelligence, edge intelligence and agents.

points.h: Foundation models are a company's job, not a school's
points.body: Why doesn't AIR do foundational general-purpose large models? Zhang Ya-Qin's reason is the resource structure: foundation models need enormous compute, data and scenarios, they need money poured in, and they need concrete scenarios — hard for a school to do. He compares them to an ecosystem's operating system, spread out horizontally. More crucial is the nature of the innovation — he believes the innovation in foundation models "is not zero-to-one innovation, it is more one-to-a-hundred, even a-hundred-to-N innovation": there is algorithmic innovation in it, but much of it is engineering innovation, which is what companies should be doing, and in the US it is also companies doing it. AIR's approach is to cooperate with enterprises and use their resources to do it.

points.h: Information intelligence is IQ; read as many books as you like, you still can't swim
points.body: Zhang Ya-Qin uses a person as an analogy: information intelligence is a person whose head is especially smart, who has read ten thousand books, who understands everything, who can solve problems, invent formulas, write articles, paint, and who understands more than the average person in every field — this is the IQ of a brain, and he judges it can be reached within five years. But "no matter how many books you read, you still won't know how to swim," you still have to swim — that is physical intelligence. He goes further: no matter how much a drinker reads or how smart he is, if he doesn't drink it still doesn't work; things in the physical world must interact with that world. The first thing to land in physical intelligence is autonomous driving, because it is a close problem; humanoid robots are an open problem and need another ten years.

points.h: Robots come in three kinds, and the home robot is the hardest
points.body: Zhang Ya-Qin himself divides robots into three scenarios: home robots, industrial robots, social robots. Home is the easiest to understand — caring for the elderly, doing housework — but the tasks are too complex and fragmented, and they involve human safety and household habits; he considers this the hardest category. Social robots are police, security guards, food delivery, driving — running on the streets and interacting a lot with everyone. Industrial robots are the easiest to define, because the goals are determined and the scenarios fixed. He hopes the back-end technology for all three kinds of robots will be common, with 70% to 80% of the back end the same, with different front ends attached on top, and the back end being one huge multimodal model.

points.h: Humanoid form is so it can use humanity's infrastructure
points.body: Why is the home robot best humanoid? Zhang Ya-Qin gives two reasons. First, interaction: if a humanoid robot looks like a person, you might not even be able to tell, the way of communicating is different, you can have heart-to-hearts with it, it becomes a companion, a butler, and it can help you care for the elderly. Second, infrastructure: our current society, staircases, buttons are all made for people, and a humanoid robot can directly use the existing infrastructure — climb stairs, press buttons. He adds that this is more a matter of choice, and the same goes for social robots — if a policeman is too small or too big you feel uncomfortable looking at it, and a humanoid form can avoid the uncanny valley effect. He also says that within ten years there may be more robots than people, and everyone will have their own copy, an avatar.

points.h: Large models relieved all three old problems of autonomous driving at once
points.body: Zhang Ya-Qin sums up the difficulties of autonomous driving over more than a decade into three: not enough test data; too many corner cases, safety scenarios you can't encounter; and technological fragmentation — one model for maps, one for vision, one for lidar, with perception, fusion, planning and decision-making pieced together block by block, mixed with rules and neural network algorithms. After large models appeared, all three were relieved at the same time: generative models can create data and simulation speeds up; large models come with common sense, so scenarios you haven't encountered can also be solved; and end-to-end puts all the models into one box, one input and one output, with rules at most as a fallback. He says Musk's end-to-end model is an important product that let everyone see the dawn.

points.h: In the past changing scenarios meant changing algorithms; now everything is Transformer
points.body: Zhang Ya-Qin points out the fundamental difference between this generation and the previous generation of deep learning: in the past you used Convolution's Cover one moment and RNN the next, different algorithms for different inputs, with the outputs then fused; now no matter what it is, it is the same Transformer, tokenized, token based. This uniformity changes the nature of the robotics problem too. Robots used to use reinforcement learning, one environment and one agent learning a policy, and applied to a physical body it often didn't work, real to sim didn't work. Their own method is called RS2, which connects the real world and the physical world, learning first in digital space and then transferring back to the real world, solving the data shortage. More crucially, large models give robots a brain — in the past robots could understand your words but not what was behind them, they had no common sense, no comprehension, no reasoning; now you can direct them to decompose a task like "take the dirty clothes to the dry cleaner" into actions.

points.h: Biological intelligence in twenty years, but consciousness won't grow out of silicon
points.body: Zhang Ya-Qin believes biological intelligence needs longer, and can be achieved within twenty years. On the path, he is more optimistic about non-invasive sensors and brain-computer interfaces, used first for treatment — stimulating neurons in the blind, stimulating hearing neurons in the deaf, repairing the central nervous system in the disabled, as well as Alzheimer's, ADHD and autism — and only afterwards extending to normal people's intelligence. But he draws a clear line: he does not think artificial intelligence can currently produce consciousness, nor does he believe there will be a new self-awareness, a new soul. The reason is that "we don't even know how we humans produce consciousness," and "we have no way to create something we don't understand." He cites Richard Feynman to support this point.

points.h: The future is a new species, but control stays in human hands
points.body: Zhang Ya-Qin's view of species: the future is a new species, only this species becomes extremely intelligent and enormously capable, but it is still an extension of humanity, controlled by humanity. He takes the Upper Cave Man of thirty thousand years ago as a reference — by then humans already had tools and fire, but the tools were very primitive; in another hundred years, looking at today's phones, internet and PCs will be like us looking at stone tools from thirty thousand years ago. He especially stresses the change in the speed of evolution: humans went from hunting to agricultural society with little change over two or three thousand years, and the real great change was the three hundred years after the Industrial Revolution; after the steam engine appeared, human evolution was no longer Darwinian natural evolution but non-linear, exponential evolution. So when he speaks of a hundred years, perhaps thirty, looking at today's humans will feel very simple.

points.h: In thirty years, driving will be like taking a carriage in New York today
points.body: Zhang Ya-Qin's concrete imagination of ten years from now: many cars are driverless, many robots enter the home, like today's refrigerators and televisions — when you're not home they help you check whether the windows are closed, whether anyone has broken in. Very few people will drive, many will choose not to drive, and the money for buying a car may be spent on buying a robot. In thirty years, seeing a person drive will be as novel as seeing a carriage in New York today, and a person driving may need special approval, a special license. He uses elevators as an analogy: thirty years ago there was still a person sitting in the elevator to press the floor for you, now there is almost none, but some places in the UK still keep manual elevators, which have instead become a kind of high-end service.

points.h: Longer lifespans will first change the work week, then population structure
points.body: Zhang Ya-Qin judges that in thirty years human lifespans will increase substantially — perhaps not immortality, but a hundred years will become the norm, and some people will reach a hundred and fifty. The social consequences he extrapolates: working hours will keep shrinking — after the Industrial Revolution people worked seven days a week, later six, and when he went abroad it was still six, and when he came back it was five, and now some places in Europe are already at four; in the future people may work one day a week and spend the rest of the time doing what they like. He stresses this is not an unemployment narrative but a matter of social productivity rising substantially and social structure changing: human lifespans grow longer, the natural birth rate falls, the number of new births shrinks, and the population of developed countries is already shrinking. He also says that in the future an eighty-year-old may still be a youth, in their prime.

terms.term: RS2 / real-to-sim then back to real
terms.def: Zhang Ya-Qin's team's method: convert real scenarios into the digital world for training, then bring them back to the real world to deploy.
Rare scenarios in autonomous driving testing that are hard to encounter yet determine safety.
Combining modules such as perception and planning into one model, where one input directly produces one output.
A model that builds and simulates the physical world in digital space, used to train embodied intelligence.
